preamble: Voicing of [s] to [z] is one of the most common consonant changes. It occurs between vowels or other voiced sounds, as in Western Romance and Old English, before voiced obstruents through regressive assimilation, as in Russian. In many languages it is allophonic; in others it became phonemic once the conditioning was lost.

examples.note: Intervocalic voicing of single /s/ in Western Romance.
The fricatives /f θ s/ had voiced allophones [v ð z] between voiced sounds after a stressed syllable; s spelled both [s] and [z].
Regressive voicing assimilation: a voiceless obstruent becomes voiced before a voiced obstruent.

All fricatives became voiced in non-final syllables; Copala (skaʔ) and Itunyoso (sikaʔ) keep s. In final syllables fricatives are usually voiced in both Chicahuaxtla and Copala, as in *rasũũ 'thing' > razũ, Copala razũũ.

sources: Matsukawa, K. (2008). Reconstruction of Proto-Trique Phonemes. University of Pennsylvania Working Papers in Linguistics 14(1), 269–281. https://repository.upenn.edu/handle/20.500.14332/44671
context: Between voiced sounds and before voiced obstruents
allophones_note: /s/ surfaces as [z] between voiced sounds (Old English, northern Italian) or before voiced obstruents (Russian), and [s] is kept elsewhere. In Portuguese and Proto-Germanic the voicing became phonemic.
